content: Acetaldehyde, also referred to as ethanal, is an organic compound with the chemical formula CH3CHO or MeCHO. It is a volatile, flammable liquid with a distinct fruity odor. This compound is naturally present in ripe fruits, coffee, and freshly baked bread, and it is also produced by plants as part of their normal metabolic processes. Acetaldehyde is widely recognized as a key contributor to hangover symptoms following alcohol consumption. In industrial applications, acetaldehyde serves as an intermediate in the synthesis of acetic acid, various esters, and other chemicals. As of 1989, the United States produced approximately 740 million pounds (336,000 metric tons) of acetaldehyde annually. One of the primary methods for its industrial production is the Wacker process. A minor fraction of acetaldehyde exists in its enol form, known as ethenol, with an equilibrium constant (Keq) of 6 x 10^-5. Ethenol has been identified in the interstellar medium, specifically in the region between the Milky Way Galaxy and the Galaxy N-ID9. In organic synthesis, acetaldehyde is a widely used two-carbon building block. Its small molecular size and availability as an anhydrous monomer make it a common electrophile. Acetaldehyde is prochiral, meaning it can participate in stereoselective reactions. It is frequently employed as a source of the CH3C+H(OH) synthon in aldol and related condensation reactions. For example, Grignard reagents and organolithium compounds react with acetaldehyde to produce hydroxyethyl derivatives. In a notable reaction, three molecules of formaldehyde react with acetaldehyde to form pentaerythritol (C(CH2OH)4). In the Strecker synthesis, acetaldehyde reacts with cyanide and ammonia to produce alanine, an amino acid, after hydrolysis. Additionally, acetaldehyde can condense with amines to form imines, such as N-ethylidenecyclohexylamine, which can direct subsequent reactions like aldol condensations. Acetaldehyde is also a precursor for synthesizing heterocyclic compounds, such as its reaction with ammonia to form 5-ethyl-2-methylpyridine, also known as aldehyde-collidine. Acetaldehyde can form acetal derivatives through condensation reactions. For instance, three molecules of acetaldehyde condense to produce paraldehyde, a cyclic trimer, while four molecules condense to form metaldehyde, another cyclic compound. When acetaldehyde reacts with ethanol under dehydrating conditions, it forms a stable acetal, CH3CH(OCH2CH3)2, commonly referred to as acetal. The term acetal is also used more broadly to describe compounds with the general formula RCH(OR')2. Biologically, acetaldehyde plays a significant role in alcohol metabolism. In the liver, the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde, which is subsequently converted into acetic acid by acetaldehyde dehydrogenase. In the final steps of alcoholic fermentation in bacteria, plants, and yeast, pyruvate is first converted into acetaldehyde by the enzyme pyruvate decarboxylase. Acetaldehyde is then reduced to ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase, operating in reverse. Acetaldehyde is closely associated with hangover symptoms. Many individuals of East Asian descent possess a genetic mutation that enhances the activity of alcohol dehydrogenase, leading to rapid conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde. However, approximately half of these individuals also have a less effective form of acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, resulting in slower conversion of acetaldehyde to acetic acid. This combination causes an accumulation of acetaldehyde after alcohol consumption, leading to the alcohol flush reaction and severe hangover symptoms. These individuals are less likely to develop alcohol dependence. The drug disulfiram (Antabuse) inhibits acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, causing similar unpleasant effects when alcohol is consumed. This mechanism has been utilized in the treatment of alcoholism. Acetaldehyde is also an environmental pollutant. It is released into the atmosphere during combustion processes, such as those occurring in automotive engines and tobacco smoking. In the case of tobacco, acetaldehyde contributes to the addictive properties of smoking. From a safety perspective, acetaldehyde is a toxic substance, an irritant, and a probable human carcinogen.
